questions.q: How many moles of carbon dioxide are in 44.0 g of CO2? (C = 12.0, O = 16.0)
questions.why: Molar mass of CO2 = 12.0 + 2(16.0) = 44.0 g/mol, so 44.0 g / 44.0 g/mol = 1.00 mol. 0.500 mol comes from dividing by 88 (doubling the formula mass by mistake); 2.00 mol comes from using 22 g/mol; 4.00 mol comes from dividing by 11.

questions.q: A balloon at 300 K is warmed to 600 K at constant pressure. What happens to its volume?
questions.why: Charles's law: V is proportional to absolute temperature at constant P, so doubling T from 300 K to 600 K doubles V. It is not unchanged because temperature is the variable being changed; it halves only if T were cut in half; quadrupling would require T to go to 1200 K.

questions.q: What is the pH of a 0.001 M solution of HCl?
questions.why: HCl is a strong acid and dissociates completely, so [H+] = 1 x 10^-3 M and pH = -log(10^-3) = 3. pH 1 corresponds to 0.1 M and pH 2 to 0.01 M. pH 11 is the pOH, not the pH, and would describe a base.

questions.q: Moving left to right across a period of the periodic table, atomic radius generally:
choices: Increases, because more electron shells are added
Stays constant, because the shell number does not change
Decreases, because nuclear charge pulls the same shell inward
questions.why: Across a period electrons are added to the same principal shell while protons are added to the nucleus, so effective nuclear charge rises and the shell is pulled tighter. New shells are added down a group, not across a period, so the first choice describes the wrong direction. The radius does change despite the constant shell number, and added electron repulsion is outweighed by the increased nuclear pull.

questions.q: For the reaction N2 + 3 H2 yields 2 NH3, you start with 1.0 mol N2 and 2.0 mol H2. Which is limiting, and how much NH3 forms?
questions.why: 1.0 mol N2 would need 3.0 mol H2, but only 2.0 mol is present, so H2 limits. 2.0 mol H2 x (2 mol NH3 / 3 mol H2) = 1.33 mol NH3. Treating N2 as limiting gives the wrong 2.0 mol answer; the pairing of H2 as limiting with 2.0 mol NH3 uses the wrong stoichiometric ratio.

questions.q: How much water must be added to 100 mL of 6.0 M HCl to make it 2.0 M?
questions.why: M1V1 = M2V2 gives (6.0)(100) = (2.0)(V2), so V2 = 300 mL total. The water ADDED is 300 - 100 = 200 mL. 300 mL is the final volume, not the water added; 100 mL and 50 mL do not satisfy the dilution equation.

questions.q: At standard temperature and pressure (273 K, 1 atm), what volume does 0.50 mol of an ideal gas occupy?
questions.why: One mole of ideal gas occupies 22.4 L at STP, so 0.50 mol occupies 11.2 L. 22.4 L is the volume for a full mole; 5.6 L corresponds to 0.25 mol; 44.8 L corresponds to 2 mol.

questions.q: A buffer contains equal molar amounts of a weak acid (pKa 4.76) and its conjugate base. What is the pH?
questions.why: Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]). With equal concentrations the log term is log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa = 4.76. 7.00 is neutral water, not a weak-acid buffer; 9.24 is 14 - 4.76, a pOH-style error; 2.38 is half the pKa, which has no basis.

questions.q: For N2(g) + 3 H2(g) in equilibrium with 2 NH3(g), increasing the pressure by decreasing the container volume will:
choices: Shift the equilibrium toward NH3, the side with fewer gas moles
Shift the equilibrium toward the reactants
Have no effect because all species are gases
questions.why: Compressing the system shifts equilibrium toward the side with fewer moles of gas: 4 mol of reactant gas versus 2 mol of product gas, so it shifts toward NH3. It does not shift toward reactants, and the effect is not zero because the mole counts differ. Kc changes only with temperature, not pressure.

questions.q: A reaction has a negative enthalpy change and a positive entropy change. It is:
questions.why: Delta G = delta H - T delta S. With delta H negative and delta S positive, both terms make delta G negative at every temperature. The high-temperature-only case applies to positive delta H with positive delta S; the low-temperature-only case applies to negative delta H with negative delta S; never spontaneous requires positive delta H with negative delta S.

questions.q: A reaction is second order in A. If [A] is tripled, the initial rate:
questions.why: Rate = k[A]^2, so tripling [A] multiplies the rate by 3^2 = 9. Tripling the rate would describe first order; no change would describe zero order; a sixfold increase would require multiplying the order by the factor instead of raising it as an exponent.

questions.q: In the reaction Zn + Cu2+ yields Zn2+ + Cu, zinc is:
choices: Oxidized, because it loses electrons and acts as the reducing agent
questions.why: Zn goes from 0 to +2, losing two electrons, so it is oxidized and serves as the reducing agent for Cu2+. It is not reduced because it loses rather than gains electrons; the oxidizing agent here is Cu2+, which is itself reduced; the oxidation state clearly changes from 0 to +2.

questions.q: Which molecule is nonpolar overall despite having polar bonds?
questions.why: CO2 is linear, so the two C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, giving zero net dipole. Water is bent and ammonia is trigonal pyramidal, so their dipoles do not cancel; HCl is a single polar bond with an obvious net dipole.

questions.q: What is the ground-state electron configuration of a neutral sulfur atom (Z = 16)?
questions.why: Sulfur has 16 electrons: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 4. The 3p6 configuration totals 18 electrons, which is argon; 3p2 totals 14, which is silicon; the 3s1 3p5 arrangement is an excited state, not the ground state, because 3s fills before 3p.

questions.q: A compound is 40.0% C, 6.7% H, and 53.3% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?
questions.why: Per 100 g: 40.0/12 = 3.33 mol C, 6.7/1 = 6.7 mol H, 53.3/16 = 3.33 mol O, a 1:2:1 ratio giving CH2O. C2H4O2, C3H6O3, and C6H12O6 are all molecular formulas with the same percentages, but the empirical formula is the smallest whole-number ratio.

questions.q: What is the mass percent of oxygen in water (H = 1.0, O = 16.0)?
questions.why: Water is 18.0 g/mol and oxygen contributes 16.0 g, so 16.0/18.0 = 0.889, or about 89%. 33% is the percent of ATOMS that are oxygen, not the mass percent; 50% ignores the mass difference between H and O; 11% is the hydrogen mass percent.

questions.q: Which aqueous solution will have the highest boiling point?
questions.why: Boiling point elevation depends on total dissolved particles. CaCl2 gives 3 particles per formula unit (3.0 m effective), NaCl gives 2 (2.0 m), glucose gives 1 (1.0 m), and 0.5 m NaCl gives only 1.0 m effective. More particles means more elevation, so CaCl2 wins.

questions.q: For AgCl, Ksp = [Ag+][Cl-]. If the molar solubility of AgCl in pure water is s, what is Ksp in terms of s?
questions.why: AgCl dissolves 1:1, so [Ag+] = [Cl-] = s and Ksp = s x s = s^2. 2s treats the ions additively rather than as a product; s ignores the second ion; 4s^3 is the expression for a 1:2 salt such as PbCl2 or Mg(OH)2.

questions.q: In the titration of a weak acid with NaOH, the pH at the equivalence point is:
choices: Greater than 7, because the conjugate base hydrolyzes water
Less than 7, because excess acid remains
Equal to the pKa of the acid
questions.why: At the equivalence point all the weak acid has been converted to its conjugate base, which reacts with water to produce OH-, giving a basic pH. A pH of exactly 7 is the equivalence point for a strong acid with a strong base; no acid remains at equivalence, so the pH is not below 7; the pH equals the pKa at the HALF-equivalence point, not the equivalence point.

questions.q: What is the conjugate base of the bicarbonate ion, HCO3-?
questions.why: A conjugate base is the species left after donating one proton, so HCO3- becomes CO3 2-. H2CO3 is the conjugate ACID of bicarbonate (it has gained a proton); CO2 is the anhydride of carbonic acid, not a conjugate pair partner differing by one proton; water is unrelated to the pair.

questions.q: A solution has pOH = 9.0 at 25 degrees C. What is its [H+]?
questions.why: pH + pOH = 14, so pH = 14 - 9 = 5 and [H+] = 1 x 10^-5 M. 1 x 10^-9 M is [OH-], obtained by forgetting to convert pOH to pH; 1 x 10^-14 M is Kw itself; 1 x 10^-7 M would be a neutral solution.

questions.q: What is the hybridization of the carbon atom in methane, CH4?
questions.why: Four sigma bonds and no lone pairs means four electron domains, which requires sp3 hybridization and tetrahedral geometry. sp corresponds to two domains (linear), sp2 to three (trigonal planar), and sp3d to five (trigonal bipyramidal), which carbon cannot form because it lacks accessible d orbitals.

questions.q: Ammonia, NH3, has four electron domains around nitrogen. What is its molecular geometry?
questions.why: The electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral, but one domain is a lone pair, so the atoms form a trigonal pyramid with bond angles near 107 degrees. Tetrahedral describes the electron domains, not the atom positions; trigonal planar requires three domains with no lone pair; bent requires two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, as in water.

questions.q: Why does water have a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide, H2S?
choices: Water has a larger molar mass
H2S has stronger London dispersion forces
Water forms hydrogen bonds; H2S cannot
questions.why: O-H bonds allow hydrogen bonding, a strong dipole-dipole interaction requiring H bonded to N, O, or F; S is not electronegative enough, so H2S relies on weaker dipole-dipole and dispersion forces. Water actually has the SMALLER molar mass (18 versus 34), water is polar not nonpolar, and H2S does have somewhat stronger dispersion forces yet still boils far lower, which is exactly the point.

questions.q: Reaction A releases 100 kJ and reaction B absorbs 40 kJ. If A and B are summed to give the overall reaction, the overall delta H is:
questions.why: Hess's law: enthalpies add, so (-100) + (+40) = -60 kJ, an exothermic overall reaction. -140 and +140 come from adding magnitudes without honoring signs; +60 reverses the sign of the sum.

questions.q: How much heat is required to raise 100 g of water from 20 to 30 degrees C? (specific heat = 4.18 J/g degree C)
questions.why: q = mc delta T = 100 g x 4.18 J/g degree C x 10 degrees C = 4180 J. 418 J uses a 1 degree change; 41,800 J uses a 100 degree change; 2090 J uses a 5 degree change.

questions.q: A gas mixture at 800 mmHg total is 20% oxygen by mole fraction. What is the partial pressure of oxygen?
questions.why: Dalton's law: partial pressure = mole fraction x total pressure = 0.20 x 800 = 160 mmHg. 80 mmHg uses 10%; 200 mmHg uses 25%; 640 mmHg is the partial pressure of everything else (80%).

questions.q: Two gases are at the same temperature. Compared with O2 (32 g/mol), helium (4 g/mol) effuses:
choices: At the same rate, because temperature is equal
questions.why: Graham's law: rate ratio = square root of (32/4) = square root of 8, which is about 2.83. Equal temperature means equal average kinetic energy, not equal speed, because the lighter gas must move faster to match that energy. Eight times faster uses the mass ratio without the square root; helium is faster, not slower.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in sulfate, SO4 2-?
questions.why: Each oxygen is -2, so 4 oxygens contribute -8; for the ion to total -2, sulfur must be +6. +4 would fit sulfite, SO3 2-; -2 is the oxidation state of sulfide, S2-; +2 does not balance the charge for any of these ions.

questions.q: In a galvanic (voltaic) cell that runs spontaneously, the cell potential and free energy change are:
choices: E cell positive, delta G negative
E cell negative, delta G negative
E cell positive, delta G positive
E cell negative, delta G positive
questions.why: delta G = -nFE, so a positive cell potential gives a negative free energy change, the signature of a spontaneous galvanic cell. A negative E with negative delta G is impossible by that equation; positive E with positive delta G is likewise contradictory; negative E with positive delta G describes an electrolytic cell that must be driven by external power.

questions.q: Adding a catalyst to a reaction at equilibrium will:
choices: Speed both forward and reverse reactions equally, leaving the equilibrium position unchanged
Lower the enthalpy change of the reaction
questions.why: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse paths by the same amount, so equilibrium is reached faster but at the same position. It does not shift the equilibrium or change K, and it does not change delta H, which depends only on the energies of reactants and products.

questions.q: According to the Arrhenius relationship, raising the temperature increases reaction rate mainly because:
choices: A larger fraction of collisions have energy exceeding the activation barrier
questions.why: Higher temperature broadens the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, so more molecules exceed Ea; collision frequency also rises but the energy fraction dominates. Temperature does not lower Ea (only a catalyst does that); heating a fixed-volume system does not raise concentration; delta H is essentially unchanged and is unrelated to rate.

questions.q: A first-order process has a half-life of 6 hours. What fraction of the original amount remains after 18 hours?
questions.why: 18 hours is three half-lives, so the remaining fraction is (1/2)^3 = 1/8. 1/3 mistakenly treats decay as linear; 1/4 is two half-lives; 1/16 is four half-lives.

questions.q: For the equilibrium 2 SO2(g) + O2(g) in equilibrium with 2 SO3(g), the correct expression for Kc is:
questions.why: K is products over reactants with each concentration raised to its coefficient: [SO3]^2 divided by [SO2]^2[O2]. The first choice inverts products and reactants; the third omits the exponents; the fourth treats coefficients as multipliers and adds rather than multiplies concentrations.

questions.q: Adding solid NaCl to a saturated solution of AgCl will:
choices: Decrease the solubility of AgCl by the common ion effect
Have no effect, because Ksp is a constant
questions.why: Added Cl- drives the equilibrium AgCl(s) in equilibrium with Ag+ + Cl- to the left, so less AgCl dissolves. Solubility falls rather than rises, and Ksp itself is unchanged because it depends only on temperature. The last choice confuses a constant Ksp with a constant solubility, which is precisely what the common ion effect changes.

questions.q: Which element has the highest first ionization energy?
questions.why: Ionization energy rises across a period and falls down a group, so among these fluorine (upper right) holds its electrons most tightly. Oxygen is close but sits one position to the left and is lower. Lithium and cesium are alkali metals that lose their single valence electron easily, cesium most easily of all.

questions.q: Which bond is most polar?
questions.why: Polarity tracks the electronegativity difference; oxygen (3.5) and hydrogen (2.1) differ by about 1.4, the largest gap here. C-C has zero difference and is nonpolar; C-H differs by only about 0.4 and is treated as essentially nonpolar in biology; C-N differs by about 0.5.

questions.q: Two isotopes of an element differ in:
choices: Number of electrons in the neutral atom
Number of neutrons, and therefore mass number
questions.why: Isotopes share atomic number but differ in neutron count, which changes mass number while chemical behavior stays nearly identical. Proton number and nuclear charge define the element, so they cannot differ; a neutral atom always has electrons equal to protons, so electron count is also the same.

questions.q: When C3H8 + O2 yields CO2 + H2O is balanced with the smallest whole numbers, the coefficient of O2 is:
questions.why: The balanced equation is C3H8 + 5 O2 yields 3 CO2 + 4 H2O: 3 carbons, 8 hydrogens, and 10 oxygens on each side. 3 and 4 are the coefficients of CO2 and H2O respectively; 7 leaves oxygen unbalanced.

questions.q: Mixing aqueous solutions of AgNO3 and NaCl produces a white precipitate. The net ionic equation is:
questions.why: Silver halides are insoluble, so Ag+ and Cl- combine while Na+ and NO3- remain dissolved as spectator ions. Sodium salts and nitrate salts are soluble, so neither NaNO3 nor AgNO3 precipitates. The full molecular equation is correct chemistry but is not the NET ionic equation, which excludes spectators.

questions.q: A molecule contains the group -COOH. Which functional group is present?
questions.why: A carbonyl bonded directly to a hydroxyl group is the carboxylic acid group. A ketone has the carbonyl flanked by two carbons; an aldehyde has a carbonyl bearing a hydrogen; an ester replaces the acidic -OH hydrogen with a carbon chain, giving -COOR.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH3?
questions.why: The longest chain is four carbons (butane) with a methyl branch; numbering from the nearer end places it at carbon 2. Pentane would require an unbranched five-carbon chain; 3-methylbutane violates the lowest-locant rule and names the same compound incorrectly; 2-methylpropane is isobutane, which has only four carbons total rather than five.

questions.q: A carbon atom is a stereocenter (chiral center) when it is bonded to:
choices: Four atoms, at least two of which are identical
Three groups and one lone pair
questions.why: Four different substituents make the mirror image non-superimposable, which is the definition of a stereocenter. Two identical groups create an internal plane of symmetry and destroy chirality; a carbon with a lone pair is a carbanion, not a standard stereocenter; a carbon with two double bonds is sp hybridized and linear, so it cannot be a stereocenter.

questions.q: Two stereoisomers have opposite configurations at ONE of their three stereocenters. They are:
questions.why: Enantiomers must differ at EVERY stereocenter; differing at some but not all makes them diastereomers, which have different physical properties. They are not identical because a configuration differs, and they are not constitutional isomers because the connectivity is the same and only spatial arrangement differs.

questions.q: In assigning R or S configuration, priority among substituents is set by:
choices: Alphabetical order of the substituent names
Size of the group in molecular weight
Atomic number at the first point of difference
questions.why: Cahn-Ingold-Prelog rules rank by atomic number of the directly attached atom, moving outward to the first point of difference if there is a tie. Alphabetical order governs how substituents are LISTED in a name, not priority; overall molecular weight and hydrogen count are not the criteria, though hydrogen is always lowest priority because its atomic number is lowest.

questions.q: A tertiary alkyl halide in a polar protic solvent with a weak nucleophile most likely reacts by:
choices: E2, requiring a strong bulky base
questions.why: Tertiary centers form stable carbocations and are too hindered for backside attack, and polar protic solvents stabilize the ion pair, so SN1 dominates and gives racemization. SN2 is blocked sterically at a tertiary carbon; a radical mechanism needs an initiator such as peroxide or light; E2 requires the strong base that the stem specifically excludes.

questions.q: Which conditions best favor an E2 elimination?
choices: Weak nucleophile, low temperature, polar protic solvent
Water as both solvent and nucleophile
Strong bulky base such as potassium tert-butoxide, with heat
questions.why: E2 is a one-step concerted elimination requiring a strong base to remove the beta hydrogen, and heat favors the entropically favorable elimination over substitution; bulky bases also steer toward elimination by resisting substitution. Weak nucleophiles in protic solvent and water alone favor SN1 or SN2; dilute acid at room temperature does not supply the base needed for E2.

questions.q: HBr adds to propene (CH3-CH=CH2). According to Markovnikov's rule, the major product is:
questions.why: The proton adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, putting the positive charge on the more substituted (secondary) carbon, so bromide lands on carbon 2. 1-bromopropane is the anti-Markovnikov product, which forms only with peroxides via a radical pathway; 1,2-dibromopropane would require Br2, not HBr; propanol requires water or hydration conditions.

questions.q: Which carbocation is most stable?
questions.why: Alkyl groups donate electron density by induction and hyperconjugation, so stability rises methyl < primary < secondary < tertiary. A vinyl cation is on an sp2 carbon with the positive charge in a high-s-character orbital and is less stable than even a primary alkyl cation.

questions.q: Resonance stabilization of the acetate ion explains why acetic acid is more acidic than ethanol because:
choices: Acetic acid has a higher molecular weight
The acetate negative charge is delocalized over two equivalent oxygens
questions.why: Spreading negative charge over two oxygens lowers the energy of the conjugate base, so the proton comes off far more readily (pKa about 4.8 versus about 16). Molecular weight does not determine acidity; ethanol is fully water-soluble; acetate has no stereocenter, and chirality is unrelated to acid strength.

questions.q: For a ring to be aromatic by Huckel's rule, it must be cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, and contain:
questions.why: Huckel's rule requires 4n + 2 pi electrons (2, 6, 10, and so on) in a continuous conjugated loop. Ring size is not fixed at six, as cyclopentadienyl anion and tropylium cation show; an even carbon count is neither necessary nor sufficient; an sp3 carbon actually BREAKS the conjugation and prevents aromaticity.

questions.q: Rank these by decreasing acidity: ethanol, phenol, acetic acid.
questions.why: Approximate pKa values are acetic acid 4.8, phenol 10, ethanol 16; carboxylate delocalizes charge over two oxygens, phenoxide over the ring only, and ethoxide not at all. Every other ordering misplaces at least one of these, most often by ranking phenol above the carboxylic acid.

questions.q: A hydrogen on the carbon next to a ketone carbonyl (an alpha hydrogen) is unusually acidic because:
choices: The alpha carbon is sp hybridized
The resulting enolate is resonance stabilized onto the carbonyl oxygen
The C-H bond is unusually long
questions.why: Removing an alpha hydrogen gives an enolate whose negative charge is shared with the electronegative carbonyl oxygen, dropping the pKa to roughly 20 versus about 50 for an ordinary alkane C-H. The alpha carbon is sp3, not sp; the carbonyl carbon is electron POOR because oxygen withdraws density; bond length is not the operative factor.

questions.q: A strong, sharp infrared absorption near 1700 cm-1 indicates:
questions.why: Carbonyl stretching gives a characteristically strong, sharp band around 1700 to 1750 cm-1. O-H appears as a broad band from 3200 to 3600 cm-1; C-C single-bond stretches are weak and fall in the crowded fingerprint region; aromatic C-H stretches appear just above 3000 cm-1.

questions.q: A very broad IR absorption from 3200 to 3600 cm-1 in a neutral compound most suggests:
choices: An alcohol O-H involved in hydrogen bonding
questions.why: Hydrogen bonding spreads the O-H stretch over a wide range of bond strengths, producing the classic broad band. A nitrile gives a sharp C-N triple-bond peak near 2250 cm-1; an alkene C=C appears near 1650 cm-1; an ether C-O falls near 1100 cm-1 and is not broad.

questions.q: In proton NMR, a signal appearing as a quartet indicates the hydrogens have:
questions.why: The n + 1 rule means the number of peaks equals neighbors plus one, so a quartet means three neighbors, the classic ethyl CH2 next to a CH3. Four neighbors would give a quintet; the multiplicity reflects NEIGHBORS, not how many hydrogens produce the signal (that is the integration); no neighbors gives a singlet.

questions.q: Which proton would appear furthest downfield (highest chemical shift) in a proton NMR spectrum?
choices: A methyl group on an alkane near 0.9 ppm
A methylene next to an ether oxygen near 3.4 ppm
questions.why: The aldehyde proton sits on a carbonyl carbon and in the deshielding cone of the C=O pi system, pushing it to about 9 to 10 ppm, the furthest downfield of these. Alkane methyls are the most shielded; vinyl and ether-adjacent protons are deshielded but far less.

questions.q: How many degrees of unsaturation does C6H10 have?
questions.why: Degrees of unsaturation = (2C + 2 - H)/2 = (12 + 2 - 10)/2 = 2, so the molecule contains two rings, two pi bonds, or one of each. One would fit C6H12; three would fit C6H8; four would fit C6H6, which is benzene.

questions.q: Heating an ester with aqueous NaOH (saponification) produces:
choices: A carboxylate salt and an alcohol
questions.why: Hydroxide attacks the ester carbonyl and the alkoxide leaves; under basic conditions the acid is deprotonated to its carboxylate salt, which makes the reaction irreversible. Amide formation requires an amine; no aldehyde is generated because the oxidation state of the carbonyl carbon is unchanged; only one alcohol is released, not two.

questions.q: The peptide bond linking two amino acids is chemically:
questions.why: The carboxyl of one residue condenses with the amino group of the next, giving a C(=O)-N amide linkage with partial double-bond character that keeps it planar. An ester requires an oxygen in place of nitrogen; an ether has no carbonyl at all; an anhydride joins two acyl groups through an oxygen, as in ATP, not in proteins.

questions.q: At physiological pH 7.4, a neutral amino acid such as glycine exists predominantly as:
questions.why: The carboxyl pKa is near 2 and the amino pKa is near 9.6, so at pH 7.4 the acid is deprotonated and the amine is protonated, giving a net-neutral zwitterion. The fully protonated form dominates well below pH 2; the fully deprotonated form dominates well above pH 9.6; the uncharged both-neutral form is essentially never significant in water.

questions.q: Alpha-D-glucose and beta-D-glucose are:
choices: Anomers, differing in configuration at the hemiacetal carbon
The same molecule in different conformations
questions.why: Ring closure creates a new stereocenter at C1, the anomeric carbon, and the two ring forms differ only there, making them anomers (a special case of diastereomers) that interconvert through the open-chain form. They are not enantiomers because all other stereocenters match; connectivity is identical, so they are not constitutional isomers; interconversion requires bond breaking, so they are not mere conformers.

questions.q: Why do unsaturated fatty acids have lower melting points than saturated fatty acids of the same chain length?
choices: They have far larger molar masses
They are ionic rather than covalent
Cis double bonds kink the chain and prevent tight packing
They form hydrogen bonds with each other
questions.why: A cis double bond puts a rigid bend in the tail, so chains cannot stack closely and dispersion forces between them are weaker, which lowers the melting point. Molar mass is essentially similar; fatty acid tails are covalent and nonpolar, not ionic; the hydrocarbon tails cannot hydrogen bond with one another.

questions.q: Rank these carboxylic acid derivatives from MOST to LEAST reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution.
questions.why: Reactivity tracks leaving-group stability and how much the attached atom donates into the carbonyl: chloride is the best leaving group and donates least, while the amide nitrogen donates strongly and is least reactive. Every other ordering inverts at least one of these, most often putting the amide too high.

questions.q: Mild oxidation of a secondary alcohol gives:
questions.why: The carbon bearing the OH has only one hydrogen, so oxidation stops at the ketone and cannot proceed further. Primary alcohols give aldehydes and then carboxylic acids with strong oxidants; tertiary alcohols have no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon and resist oxidation; reduction, not oxidation, would move toward an alkane.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts sodium borohydride (NaBH4) with lithium aluminum hydride (LiAlH4)?
choices: NaBH4 reduces esters but LiAlH4 does not
NaBH4 is milder and reduces aldehydes and ketones but not esters or carboxylic acids
LiAlH4 is safe to use in water
questions.why: NaBH4 is a selective, mild hydride source that handles aldehydes and ketones and tolerates protic solvents, while LiAlH4 is far stronger and reduces esters, amides, and carboxylic acids. The first choice reverses their capabilities; both are reducing agents, not oxidizers; LiAlH4 reacts violently with water and requires dry ether conditions.

questions.q: A Grignard reagent (R-MgBr) reacting with formaldehyde, followed by aqueous workup, gives:
questions.why: The carbanion-like R group attacks the formaldehyde carbonyl, and protonation on workup gives R-CH2-OH, a primary alcohol. Other aldehydes give secondary alcohols and ketones or esters give tertiary alcohols; a carboxylic acid results only from quenching the Grignard with CO2; no ketone survives because the alkoxide is the direct product.

questions.q: Fischer esterification combines a carboxylic acid and an alcohol under acid catalysis to give:
questions.why: Acid activates the carbonyl, the alcohol adds, and water leaves, so the products are the ester and water; the reaction is reversible and is driven by removing water or adding excess alcohol. Amides require an amine, aldehydes require reduction or oxidation chemistry rather than condensation, and acid chlorides require reagents such as thionyl chloride.

questions.q: Which of these is an alkyne?
choices: C4H6 with a carbon-carbon triple bond
questions.why: An alkyne contains a carbon-carbon triple bond and, if acyclic with one triple bond, fits CnH2n-2, which C4H6 satisfies. C4H8 fits an alkene or cycloalkane, C4H10 is a saturated alkane, and C4H10O is a saturated alcohol or ether.

questions.q: In the most stable chair conformation of methylcyclohexane, the methyl group is:
choices: Axial, because axial positions are lower in energy
Either, since the two chairs are equal in energy
questions.why: An axial substituent crowds the two axial hydrogens on the same face three carbons away, so the equatorial chair is favored by roughly 1.7 kcal/mol for a methyl group. Axial is not intrinsically lower in energy, and the strain relieved is steric rather than torsional, so the two chairs are not equal.

questions.q: How many constitutional isomers does C4H10 have?
questions.why: C4H10 exists as n-butane and isobutane (2-methylpropane) only. There is more than one because branching is possible; a third or fourth structure would require repeating one of these two, since drawing the methyl branch at a different position just renames the same molecule.

questions.q: An alcohol whose carbinol carbon is attached to two other carbons is classified as:
questions.why: Classification counts carbons attached to the carbon bearing the OH: two makes it secondary. Primary has one (or zero, as in methanol), tertiary has three, and phenolic means the OH is attached directly to an aromatic ring, which is a separate category with markedly different acidity.

questions.q: In IUPAC naming, which functional group takes highest priority for the suffix of the parent name?
questions.why: The standard priority order runs carboxylic acid > ester > amide > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine, so the carboxylic acid claims the suffix and the lowest locant. Ketones, alcohols, and amines all rank lower and would be cited as prefixes (oxo-, hydroxy-, amino-) when an acid is present.

questions.q: Benzene reacts with Br2 and FeBr3 to give bromobenzene rather than an addition product because:
choices: Benzene has no pi electrons to donate
Bromine is too large to add
Substitution preserves the aromatic ring and its stabilization energy
The reaction is a free radical chain
questions.why: Addition across the ring would destroy aromaticity and cost roughly 36 kcal/mol of resonance stabilization, so the arenium intermediate loses a proton instead and restores the aromatic system. Benzene is rich in pi electrons and attacks the electrophile; size is not the barrier; the mechanism is electrophilic aromatic substitution, not a radical chain.

questions.q: The high energy released when ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP comes mainly from cleavage of:
choices: A phosphoanhydride bond between phosphate groups
questions.why: The terminal phosphoanhydride bond joins two phosphates whose adjacent negative charges repel; hydrolysis relieves that repulsion and the products gain resonance stabilization and solvation. The ribose-phosphate linkage is a lower-energy ester bond, the adenine linkage is a glycosidic bond that is not the energy source, and ATP contains no peptide bond.

questions.q: In a right-skewed (positively skewed) distribution of hospital lengths of stay, which is true?
choices: The mean is greater than the median
The median is greater than the mean
The mode is the largest value
questions.why: A long right tail of a few very long stays pulls the mean upward while the median, a rank-based measure, resists them. Mean equals median in a symmetric distribution; median above mean describes LEFT skew; the mode sits at the peak on the left side, not at the largest value.

questions.q: What is the median of 3, 7, 8, 12, 15, 20?
questions.why: With six ordered values the median is the average of the third and fourth: (8 + 12)/2 = 10. Choosing 8 or 12 alone takes only one middle value; 10.83 would be the mean, which here happens to be close but is a different statistic.

questions.q: Which measure of central tendency can be used with nominal data such as blood type?
questions.why: The mode is the most frequent category and is the only one of these that requires no ordering or arithmetic. The mean requires numeric values, the median requires a meaningful rank order, and the standard deviation is a measure of spread, not center, and also requires numeric data.

questions.q: Two classes have the same mean exam score, but class A has a standard deviation of 4 and class B has 12. This means:
choices: Class A scored higher on average
Class A has a higher maximum score
Class B scores are more spread out around the mean
questions.why: Standard deviation measures dispersion, so a larger value means scores sit further from the mean on average. The means are stated to be equal, so neither class scored higher; sample size is not determined by the standard deviation; class B, with the wider spread, is actually likelier to contain the highest score.

questions.q: A dataset has a variance of 25. What is its standard deviation?
questions.why: Standard deviation is the square root of variance, so the square root of 25 is 5. 25 is the variance itself; 625 is the variance squared; 12.5 is half the variance and has no statistical meaning here.

questions.q: A dataset has Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 40. Using the 1.5 x IQR rule, a value is an outlier if it is:
questions.why: IQR = 40 - 20 = 20, and 1.5 x 20 = 30, so the fences are 20 - 30 = -10 and 40 + 30 = 70. The first choice just restates the quartiles; 0 and 60 use 1.0 x IQR; 10 and 50 use 0.5 x IQR.

questions.q: Serum sodium is normally distributed with mean 140 and standard deviation 2 mEq/L. About what percentage of people fall between 136 and 144?
questions.why: 136 and 144 are two standard deviations from the mean, and the empirical rule puts about 95% of a normal distribution within 2 SD. 68% covers 1 SD (138 to 142), 99.7% covers 3 SD (134 to 146), and 50% would be everything on one side of the mean.

questions.q: A patient's cholesterol is 230 mg/dL in a population with mean 200 and standard deviation 20. What is the z-score?
questions.why: z = (230 - 200)/20 = 30/20 = 1.5. A z of 3.0 would require a value of 260; 1.15 comes from dividing 230 by 200; 0.65 has no valid derivation from these numbers.

questions.q: A sample has standard deviation 10 and n = 100. What is the standard error of the mean?
questions.why: SEM = s divided by the square root of n = 10 / 10 = 1.0. 10 is the sample standard deviation, not the standard error; 0.1 divides by n instead of the square root of n; 100 is n itself.

questions.q: The central limit theorem states that as sample size increases, the sampling distribution of the mean:
choices: Becomes identical to the population distribution
Approaches a normal distribution regardless of the population's shape
questions.why: The theorem applies to the distribution of SAMPLE MEANS, which becomes approximately normal as n grows even when the underlying population is skewed. It does not mirror the population distribution, it does not become uniform, and the standard error DECREASES with larger n because it divides by the square root of n.

questions.q: A study reports a mean systolic blood pressure reduction of 8 mmHg with a 95% confidence interval of 2 to 14 mmHg. The best interpretation is:
choices: 95% of patients had reductions between 2 and 14 mmHg
There is a 95% chance the next patient drops 8 mmHg
The result is not statistically significant
We are 95% confident the true mean reduction lies between 2 and 14 mmHg, and since the interval excludes 0 the result is significant at alpha 0.05
questions.why: A confidence interval is about the population PARAMETER, not individual patients, and an interval for a difference that excludes 0 corresponds to p below 0.05. The first choice confuses the CI with a range covering individuals; the second misapplies it to a single future patient; the third is wrong because 0 is outside the interval.

questions.q: Which change would make a confidence interval narrower?
choices: Increasing the confidence level from 95% to 99%
Increasing the variability in the data
questions.why: Width depends on the standard error, which shrinks as the square root of n grows, so a larger sample narrows the interval. Raising the confidence level requires a larger critical value and widens it; more variability raises the standard deviation and widens it; a smaller sample widens it.

questions.q: A p-value of 0.03 means:
choices: There is a 3% probability the null hypothesis is true
The treatment effect is 3% in size
If the null hypothesis were true, there is a 3% probability of data at least this extreme
There is a 97% chance the alternative hypothesis is true
questions.why: The p-value is a conditional probability computed ASSUMING the null is true; it says nothing directly about the probability of either hypothesis. It is not the probability the null is true, not the probability the alternative is true, and not a measure of effect size, which is why effect estimates and confidence intervals are reported alongside it.

questions.q: A type I error occurs when a researcher:
choices: Fails to reject a false null hypothesis
Correctly rejects a false null hypothesis
questions.why: A type I error is a false positive: concluding an effect exists when it does not, with probability alpha. Failing to reject a false null is a type II error; correctly rejecting a false null is power, not an error; small sample size affects power but is not itself a type I error.

questions.q: The power of a study is:
choices: The probability of a type I error
The size of the treatment effect
The probability of correctly detecting a true effect, equal to 1 minus beta
questions.why: Power is the chance of rejecting the null when the alternative is truly correct, and it rises with larger samples, larger effects, and less variability. Alpha is the type I error rate, not power; effect size is an input to the power calculation rather than power itself.

questions.q: In a trial comparing a new drug with placebo, the null hypothesis states that:
choices: There is no difference between the groups in the population
questions.why: The null is the statement of no effect or no difference, which the data are used to try to refute. Superiority and inferiority are alternative hypotheses (one-sided versions at that), and equal sample sizes are a design feature, not a hypothesis being tested.

questions.q: Compared with a two-tailed test at the same alpha, a one-tailed test:
choices: Can detect effects in either direction
Has more power to detect an effect in the prespecified direction but none in the other
questions.why: Putting the entire alpha in one tail lowers the critical value for that direction, so it is easier to reach significance there, but an effect in the opposite direction can never be declared significant. It cannot detect effects in either direction, its p-value in the predicted direction is typically half the two-tailed value rather than larger, and it needs a smaller, not larger, sample.

questions.q: A researcher sets alpha at 0.05. If she runs 20 independent tests on data with no real effects, roughly how many false positives should she expect?
questions.why: Alpha is the false positive rate per test, so 20 x 0.05 = 1 expected false positive; this is the multiple comparisons problem that corrections such as Bonferroni address. Zero ignores the definition of alpha; 5 would be 25% of tests; 20 would mean every test is a false positive.

questions.q: You want to compare mean hemoglobin between two independent groups of patients. The appropriate test is:
questions.why: A continuous outcome compared between two separate groups calls for an independent samples t-test. Chi-square is for categorical counts; Pearson correlation measures association between two continuous variables in the same subjects rather than comparing group means; a paired t-test is for two measurements on the SAME subjects.

questions.q: A one-way ANOVA comparing mean blood pressure across four drug groups returns p = 0.002. This tells you:
choices: Every group differs from every other group
Drug A is the most effective
At least one group mean differs from the others, but not which one
questions.why: ANOVA is an omnibus test: it detects that some difference exists but requires post hoc comparisons such as Tukey to identify which pairs differ. It does not establish that all pairs differ, does not rank the drugs, and says nothing about variances, which are in fact ASSUMED to be equal.

questions.q: A correlation coefficient of r = -0.85 indicates:
questions.why: The sign gives direction and the magnitude gives strength, so -0.85 is a strong inverse linear association. Weak would be a magnitude near 0.1 to 0.3; no relationship would be near 0; the negative sign rules out a positive relationship.

questions.q: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly correlated across months. The best explanation is:
choices: The correlation must be a calculation error
A confounder, hot weather, drives both
questions.why: A third variable associated with both exposure and outcome produces a non-causal association; correlation alone never establishes causation. Neither causal direction is plausible, and the correlation is real rather than a computational mistake, which is exactly why confounding must be considered.

questions.q: In a linear regression, r squared = 0.36. This means:
choices: 36% of the variance in the outcome is explained by the predictor
The slope of the line is 0.36
questions.why: The coefficient of determination is the proportion of outcome variance accounted for by the model. The correlation here is the square root of 0.36, which is 0.6 in magnitude; r squared is not an accuracy rate for individual predictions and is not the slope, which carries units of the variables.

questions.q: A regression of weight (kg) on height (cm) yields slope = 0.8. This means that for each additional centimeter of height:
choices: Predicted weight increases by 0.8 kg on average
questions.why: A slope is the average change in the outcome per one-unit change in the predictor, in the outcome's units. It is not a total value, not a percentage change, and not a measure of explained variance, which would be r squared.

questions.q: If two events are independent, with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5, what is P(A and B)?
questions.why: For independent events probabilities multiply: 0.4 x 0.5 = 0.2. 0.9 adds them, which is the rule for the union of mutually exclusive events; 0.1 subtracts them; 0.45 averages them.

questions.q: In a clinic, 30% of patients have diabetes and 12% have both diabetes and hypertension. What is the probability a patient has hypertension GIVEN diabetes?
questions.why: P(H given D) = P(H and D)/P(D) = 0.12/0.30 = 0.40. 0.12 is the joint probability without conditioning; 0.30 is the prevalence of diabetes; 0.42 adds the two probabilities, which is not a conditional probability.

questions.q: Events A and B are mutually exclusive, with P(A) = 0.25 and P(B) = 0.35. What is P(A or B)?
questions.why: For mutually exclusive events P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.25 + 0.35 = 0.60, with no overlap to subtract. 0.0875 multiplies them, which would apply to independent events and their intersection; 0.10 subtracts; 0.30 averages.

questions.q: If the probability that a patient responds to a drug is 0.3, what is the probability that a patient does NOT respond?
questions.why: The complement rule gives 1 - 0.3 = 0.7. 0.3 restates the original probability; 0.09 is 0.3 squared, which would be the chance two independent patients both respond; probabilities cannot exceed 1, so 1.3 is impossible.

questions.q: A binomial setting requires all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: A constant probability of success across independent trials
questions.why: The binomial model describes counts of successes in categorical trials, so a continuous normal outcome is the one condition that does NOT apply. Fixed trial count, exactly two outcomes, and independent trials with constant success probability are the four defining requirements.

questions.q: A researcher divides a population into age bands and randomly samples within each band. This is:
questions.why: Stratified sampling divides the population into meaningful subgroups and samples randomly within each, which guarantees representation across age. Cluster sampling randomly selects whole naturally occurring groups and samples all members; systematic sampling takes every kth unit from a list; convenience sampling uses whoever is easiest to reach and is not random at all.

questions.q: A survey on hospital satisfaction is given only to patients still admitted on a Friday afternoon. The main problem is:
choices: Selection bias, so the sample may not represent all patients
questions.why: Patients still hospitalized on a given afternoon differ systematically from those already discharged, so the sample is not representative and results will not generalize. A type I error is a false positive on a test, not a sampling flaw; more data would not fix a biased sampling frame; confounding by indication concerns treatment assignment, not survey recruitment.

questions.q: Which study design provides the strongest evidence that a treatment CAUSES an outcome?
questions.why: Randomization balances known and unknown confounders across groups and establishes that exposure preceded outcome, which is what supports a causal claim. A case series has no comparison group; a cross-sectional survey measures exposure and outcome at one moment and cannot establish temporality; a case-control study is observational and starts from the outcome.

questions.q: Why is a case-control study reported with an odds ratio rather than a relative risk?
choices: Odds ratios are always larger and look more impressive
Case-control studies have no control group
Relative risk cannot be computed for rare diseases
Subjects are selected by outcome status, so true incidence and therefore risk cannot be calculated
questions.why: The investigator fixes how many cases and controls to enroll, so the proportion who develop disease is an artifact of the design and incidence is unknowable; the odds ratio can still be computed and approximates relative risk when the disease is rare. Odds ratios are not chosen for impressiveness, controls are by definition present, and relative risk is computable for rare diseases in cohort designs.

questions.q: In a cohort study, 20 of 100 exposed subjects and 10 of 100 unexposed subjects develop disease. What is the relative risk?
questions.why: RR = (20/100) / (10/100) = 0.20/0.10 = 2.0, so exposure doubles the risk. 0.5 inverts the ratio; 10 is the absolute risk difference expressed as 10 percentage points, not a ratio; 1.1 has no valid derivation.

questions.q: An event occurs in 10% of treated patients and 20% of controls. What is the number needed to treat?
questions.why: Absolute risk reduction = 0.20 - 0.10 = 0.10, and NNT = 1/ARR = 10 patients treated to prevent one event. 5 would follow from an ARR of 0.20; 2 comes from the relative risk of 2.0 rather than the absolute difference; 20 uses 1/0.05.

questions.q: A test detects 90 of 100 patients who truly have the disease. This describes:
questions.why: Sensitivity is true positives divided by all who actually have the disease: 90/100 = 90%. Specificity is calculated among people WITHOUT the disease; PPV is calculated among people who test positive; NPV is calculated among people who test negative. All three of those use different denominators.

questions.q: A highly SPECIFIC test is most useful clinically to:
choices: Screen a large healthy population for rare disease
Replace the gold standard test entirely
Rule IN disease when the result is positive
Rule OUT disease when the result is negative
questions.why: High specificity means few false positives, so a positive result strongly confirms disease (the SpPIn rule). Ruling out with a negative result is what a highly SENSITIVE test does (SnNOut), which is also why sensitive tests are preferred for screening; and no index test replaces the gold standard, which defines the truth it is measured against.

questions.q: The same test with fixed sensitivity and specificity is moved from a high-prevalence clinic to a low-prevalence screening setting. What happens?
choices: Nothing changes, because all four measures are test properties
Positive predictive value falls while negative predictive value rises
questions.why: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test itself, but predictive values depend on pretest probability: with fewer true cases, more positives are false, so PPV drops while NPV climbs. Sensitivity and specificity do not change with prevalence, and the claim that nothing changes ignores that PPV and NPV are not intrinsic test properties.

questions.q: Which technique best controls for confounding at the DESIGN stage of a study?
choices: Randomization of subjects to treatment groups
questions.why: Randomization distributes both measured and unmeasured confounders evenly between groups before any outcome occurs; restriction and matching are other design-stage tools, while multivariable adjustment works at the analysis stage. A larger sample reduces random error but not systematic bias; confidence intervals describe precision; a one-tailed test only changes how significance is judged.

questions.q: In a double-blind trial, who is unaware of treatment assignment?
choices: Both the participants and the investigators assessing outcomes
questions.why: Double blinding conceals assignment from participants and from the investigators or assessors, which limits both placebo effects and biased outcome assessment. Blinding participants alone is single blinding; blinding investigators alone is also single blinding; blinding the analysts is an additional layer sometimes called triple blinding.
